amendments.rule: **A cognate infinitive absolute the ASV renders with a distinct adverbial word takes that word as its own unit.** The finite cognate verb retains its subject, auxiliaries and lexical verb phrase under rule 17, while the infinitive absolute takes the English word spent on its emphasis and heads on that word: `פָּקֹד יִפְקֹד` → *will surely visit* gives *surely* to the infinitive absolute and *will visit* to the finite verb, and `הָשֵׁב יָשִׁיב` → *will fully requite* gives *fully* and *will requite* on the same terms. This is rule 2's smallest defensible unit rather than rule 30 fusion, because the ASV has written a separate English word for the infinitive absolute's contribution. The finished corpus has 34 Qal infinitive-absolute units across 26 chapters independently aligned to *surely*, *utterly*, *indeed*, *diligently* or *certainly*, all headed on the intensifier. **Read that word as whatever the ASV has spent on the emphasis, and not as a class of intensifying adverbs.** Where the clause is a rhetorical, concessive or conditional one and the ASV writes a minimizing or restrictive adverb in that same slot, the word is the infinitive absolute's on exactly the same terms and heads its unit: `וְאָבִיהָ יָרֹק יָרַק בְּפָנֶיהָ` → *If her father had* ***but*** *spit in her face* gives *but* to the infinitive absolute and *had spit* to the finite verb. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do: drop the English word and ask whether the infinitive absolute has lost its whole rendering or only the clause has lost a shade of force. Do not mark such a word `added` under rule 30 or fold it into the finite verb, into a conjunction or into a negative standing beside it, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*: a morpheme stands in the clause for it, no other morpheme answers to it, and the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. Where the ASV writes no distinct adverbial word at all for the infinitive absolute, the ordinary rules decide what, if anything, realizes it.
amendments.why: NUM.12.14 renders יָרֹק יָרַק as *had but spit*. The infinitive absolute's English word is a minimizer, not an intensifier, and nothing else in וְאָבִיהָ יָרֹק יָרַק בְּפָנֶיהָ can carry it: the waw holds *If* under rule 55, the noun and its suffix hold *her father*, and the preposition and its noun hold *in her face*. Rule 56 as written tests for an 'intensifier' three times, and its closing sentence hands a clause with no intensifier to the ordinary rules, where a careful pass would mark *but* `added` under rule 30 or fold it into the finite verb — both wrong, since a morpheme licenses it. The amendment widens the test term to what the ASV spent on the emphasis, adds the subtraction test the contract uses elsewhere, and names the fold-avoidance the rule did not previously block. It contradicts nothing: the 34 corpus units the rule cites are all still governed by the same sentence, and the widening only reaches words those units do not contain.

conventions: A construct numeral carrying a pronominal suffix splits: the numeral takes its own English word and the suffix takes the bare personal pronoun the ASV writes beside it, headed on that pronoun. שְׁלָשְׁתְּכֶם gives three to the numeral and ye to the suffix (12.4), שְׁלָשְׁתָּם gives three and they (12.4), שְׁנֵיהֶם gives both and they (12.5). This is rule 19's bare-pronoun sentence handing the case to rule 18. The competing reading gives they to the finite 3mp verb under rule 17 and leaves the suffix unrepresented; 12.4's ye three, which no third-person verb could carry, fixes the reading and the two they phrases follow it.

מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה is divided the same way at 12.14 and 12.15: מִן and חוּץ share one unit rendered by the single word without, headed on חוּץ (rule 30); the לְ is unrepresented, the ASV writing no word for its own relation (rule 40, and its סָבִיב לַמִּשְׁכָּן case); and the article assimilated into the pointed לַ takes the written the (rule 12). BSB attaches the לְ to its phrase and disagrees at both verses.

נָא takes whatever entreaty the ASV writes at that point and nothing more — now (12.6), I pray thee (12.11), I pray (12.12), I beseech thee (12.13) — the formula's pronouns being the particle's under rule 30 and an absent object simply not aligned. Where one verse writes the particle twice for a single English formula, as 12.13's אֵל נָא … רְפָא נָא does, the occurrence standing with the imperative the entreaty attaches to takes the formula and the other is unrepresented under rule 22; the competing reading assigns it to the first.

report: All 26 candidate lemma groups checked. Every bucket showing two treatments is licensed by a difference the ASV wrote, not by a split: the same בְּמֹשֶׁה is rendered against (12.1), with (12.2) and against (12.8); the waw takes And, Now, and, even, if and then off rule 14's open list; אָמַר is spake in 12.4 and said in 12.11/12.14; אֶל is unto six times and upon in 12.10 (looked upon Miriam); הֲ takes Hath (12.2) and should (12.14).

The three article buckets are ASV-driven and correct under rule 29's closing sentence: the article is unrepresented exactly where the ASV writes no the (12.6 in a vision, 12.10 as snow) and takes it where one is written (12.14, 12.15 the camp). 12.12's [הַ] to one is a substantival article on a participle under rule 41 — a different construction, not a third treatment of the same one.

Read the dump end to end for the added-vs-folded asymmetry the table is blind to. The chapter's only two added units are 12.2's supplied object pronoun it (no object morpheme in וַיִּשְׁמַע יְהוָה, rule 44) and 12.10's italic white as. Every other supplied English word is folded onto the morpheme that licenses it, consistently across all sixteen verses: indefinite a onto its noun (12.1, 12.5, 12.6 three times), construct the onto the construct noun (12.4, 12.8, 12.9, 12.16), copulas onto predicates (12.3, 12.7 twice, 12.10 twice), subject pronouns and the volitive Let onto their verbs (12.12, 12.14), phrasal out / forth / up / in again onto their verbs (12.4, 12.5, 12.12, 12.14, 12.15). No verse marks added what another folds.

Parallel constructions across verses are aligned identically: מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה at 12.14 and 12.15; שִׁבְעַת יָמִים written and rendered in full at all three occurrences, so rule 22 reaches none; Niphal אָסַף and סָגַר keeping the phrasal particle with the verb in both verses; the numeral-plus-suffix phrases at 12.4 (twice) and 12.5; construct chains with an arthrous rectum taking the article's own the plus a supplied one (12.3, 12.5) against those with a bare-name or anarthrous rectum taking a supplied the alone (12.4, 12.8, 12.9, 12.16).

BSB: all seven disagreements are documented convention differences and none is a genuine error. 12.1 הַ is the agreement article on הַכֻּשִׁית, unrepresented under rule 41's prenominal-attributive sentence and rule 47. 12.14 and 12.15 לַ are rule 40's own סָבִיב לַמִּשְׁכָּן case, where a two-word rendering (without / round about) belongs whole to the adverb and the preposition keeps nothing. 12.13 לָהּ is rule 40's תְּנָה לִּי case, a dative recast as a bare English object. 12.13 נָא is the first of two the ASV renders once (rule 22). 12.12 וַ is a waw the ASV leaves unrendered inside a relative אֲשֶׁר has already opened, and 12.12 וֹ is the resumptive suffix in that same clause, both defensible with the competing reading already named in the verse notes.

One amendment returned, to rule 56. 12.14's יָרֹק יָרַק is rendered had but spit: the infinitive absolute's word is a minimizer, not an intensifier, and rule 56's test term would send a literal reader to the ordinary rules, where nothing else in the clause answers for but and it would be marked added. The rule is rewritten to read what the ASV spent on the emphasis rather than a class of adverbs. Three conventions logged; no patches.
